clue.text: Distort the French dollar exchange

indicators.note: exchange tells you to swap the order of the two pieces as the clue gives them

parts.note: a buck is slang for a dollar
le is the French masculine word for 'the'

explanation.surface: Someone describes swapping euros or dollars at a French bureau de change.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue lists 'the French' before 'dollar'; 'exchange' asks you to swap them, so BUCK comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: To buckle a wheel or sheet of metal is to bend it out of shape, a direct synonym.

clue.text: One's carried for the rest of the trek

definitions.text: One's carried for the rest of the trek

parts.words: One's carried for the rest of the trek
parts.note: the 'rest' is not the remainder of the journey but the night's sleep, so this is what a hiker carries to lie on

explanation.surface: A porter is handed one load to carry for the remaining miles of a long hike.
explanation.definitionFit: A rolled-up sleeping bag or blanket is carried by hikers so they can rest at night.

clue.text: Sign of 19's commitment

parts.note: the Christian symbol that shows the faith of an archbishop of Canterbury

explanation.surface: Something shows how dedicated a particular figure is.
explanation.walkthrough: 19 is CANTUAR, the signature of the Archbishop of Canterbury; the Christian symbol stands for his faith, and he is also blessed by making the sign with his hand.
explanation.definitionFit: The crucifix emblem is the chief sign of Christian faith, which an archbishop carries and wears.

clue.text: 19's connection with Westminster?

parts.note: the archbishop's London home sits across the Thames from Parliament, and a river crossing named after his palace links them

explanation.surface: Someone asks how a churchman links up with the seat of political power.
explanation.walkthrough: 19 is CANTUAR, the Archbishop of Canterbury, whose London residence is Lambeth Palace; the bridge named after it crosses the Thames to Westminster. 'Connection' sounds like influence but is a literal span.
explanation.definitionFit: The bridge next to the archbishop's palace spans the river to Westminster, physically connecting the two.

clue.text: 's "a hairy man", speaking in child's play

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held reads ''s "a hairy man", speaking in child's play' and begins with a bare 's: a word before it is missing (the homophone presumably needs SEES + ESAU), and a quoted search found no fuller text.
annotationWithheld.clue: 's "a hairy man", speaking in child's play

clue.text: They are powerless to follow Brussels! Name such characters!

parts.note: Brussels is the seat of the European Union, EU

indicators.note: characters invites you to treat the letters of such as rearrangeable characters

explanation.surface: An exclamation mocks a group of officials who simply do whatever Brussels decides.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface jokes that people who merely obey Brussels have no power; 'characters' is the rearrangement signal, taking the letters of 'such' as characters to reorder.
explanation.definitionFit: Castrated men are, figuratively and literally, without potency or power.

clue.text: Happiest time singularly bounded by bell-ringers?

definitions.text: Happiest time singularly bounded by bell-ringers?

parts.words: Happiest time singularly bounded by bell-ringers?
parts.note: the saying calls the years of lessons 'the happiest days of your life'; singularly means take just one, and the bells ringing start and end it

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a period of joy is enclosed by the peals of a church tower.
explanation.walkthrough: The saying is 'your schooldays are the happiest days of your life'; 'singularly' asks for one day, which begins and ends with a school bell.
explanation.definitionFit: A single day at school, framed by bells, is the singular of the proverbial happiest days.

clue.text: Just came fourth did he?

parts.note: points both to Richmal Crompton's schoolboy hero of the 'Just ...' books and to the king who was the fourth of that name

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a runner only scraped into fourth place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Just William' is a series of British children's books; William IV was the fourth king so named. 'Just' and 'came fourth' read like a race result.
explanation.definitionFit: The name fits both the Just books' boy hero and King William IV, the fourth monarch so called.

clue.text: Growth in this Riley's biography

definitions.meaning: a plant, the three-leaved forage crop that grows in meadows
'the life of Riley' means a carefree, luxurious existence, also called living in this plant

explanation.surface: Something grows inside a book about a man named Riley.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Living in clover' and 'the life of Riley' are both idioms for an easy, prosperous life.
explanation.definitionFit: The trefoil is a growing plant, and to be in it is the idiom matching the life of Riley.

clue.text: Work of Keats? No, a Cholmondeley construction

indicators.note: construction means the letters are built into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A poem attributed to Keats turns out to be by someone with the grand surname Cholmondeley.
explanation.walkthrough: Cholmondeley is an English surname pronounced 'Chumley', which hides how many letters it gives.
explanation.definitionFit: Keats wrote this 1819 ode, one of his best-known poems.

clue.text: Burns on the face of a haggis: is nose broken?

definitions.text: Burns on the face of a haggis

indicators.note: broken means the letters of the two words are smashed and reassembled

explanation.surface: Someone sees a burn mark on a haggis and asks whether its nose is broken.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Burns, in 'To a Haggis', writes 'Fair fa' your honest, sonsie face'; Burns here is the poet, not injuries.
explanation.definitionFit: Burns used this Scots word, meaning plump and jolly, to describe the haggis's face.

clue.text: No end of depravity to reveal over 7's niece

indicators.note: no end of means drop the final letter of the word for depravity

parts.note: vice is wickedness or depravity
taken as written

indicators.note: over means the word for reveal is turned backwards

parts.note: to air something is to make it public

explanation.surface: Someone resolves to expose all manner of wickedness about a relative's niece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No end of' cuts VICE to VIC; 'over' turns AIR into RIA. 7 is WILLIAM: Queen Victoria was William IV's niece.
explanation.definitionFit: Queen Victoria was the daughter of William IV's brother, so she was his niece.

clue.text: One embracing an argumentative settler

definitions.meaning: someone who holds another in a clinch, a tight hug
a decisive point that ends a dispute

explanation.surface: A colonist who likes arguing hugs someone.
explanation.definitionFit: A clinch is an embrace, and a decisive point that wins an argument is called a clincher.

clue.text: Immature tone, no use orchestrating

indicators.note: orchestrating means arranging, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A musician says a juvenile tone cannot be fixed by scoring it for orchestra.
explanation.definitionFit: In biology the term describes animals keeping juvenile features into adulthood, hence immature.

clue.text: Thus solve the setter's irregularity to nab an Oscar

parts.note: so means thus
to do a puzzle is to solve it
the setter refers to himself, so the setter's is my

explanation.surface: A setter asks you to work out his puzzle's quirk in order to win an award.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition alludes to Oscar Wilde, imprisoned for his homosexuality; 'Oscar' looks like the letter O or an award.
explanation.definitionFit: The sexual act once outlawed was the kind of conduct for which Oscar Wilde was convicted.

clue.text: 11 2 for this

parts.note: the queen's decoration from the two cross-references bears the inscription 'For ...' naming the quality it rewards

explanation.surface: A cross-reference clue pointing at two other answers.
explanation.walkthrough: 11 and 2 are VICTORIA and CROSS: the Victoria Cross, Britain's highest military award, is inscribed 'For Valour'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Victoria Cross is awarded for bravery, the quality engraved on the medal.

clue.text: State region doesn't end in song

indicators.note: in means the shortened region goes inside the word for song

parts.note: an aria is a song in opera

indicators.note: doesn't end means the last letter of the region word is dropped

parts.note: a zone is a region

explanation.surface: A region of the country never stops singing about itself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'doesn't end' cuts ZONE to ZON, which goes 'in' ARIA.
explanation.definitionFit: Arizona is one of the fifty states of the USA.

clue.text: One responding to the nuclear debate?

definitions.text: One responding to the nuclear debate?

parts.words: One responding to the nuclear debate?
parts.note: reads as a person reacting to arguments about atomic power, but is the atomic power plant's core itself

explanation.surface: Someone joins in the argument over atomic energy.
explanation.walkthrough: A person who responds is a reactor; so is the core of a nuclear power station, at the centre of the debate.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally one that reacts, and also the vessel in which nuclear fission is controlled.

clue.text: My exclusion zone against space invaders?

definitions.text: My exclusion zone against space invaders?

parts.words: My exclusion zone against space invaders?
parts.note: the NIMBY's cry 'not in my ...' marks the patch they keep developers out of; space invaders also suggests the video game

explanation.surface: Someone talks about defending their territory against alien attackers.
explanation.walkthrough: NIMBY stands for 'not in my back yard', said by residents objecting to building near home.
explanation.definitionFit: The garden behind a house is the area a NIMBY guards against unwanted development.

clue.text: Home visit requested from this little 7, inventor of a 26

definitions.text: Home visit requested from this little 7
definitions.meaning: the song 'Won't You Come Home, Bill ...' asks a man with the short form of William to return
Sir Donald ..., who designed the portable military bridge named after him

explanation.surface: A small boy is asked to come home by someone who invented a crossing.
explanation.walkthrough: 7 is WILLIAM, and 'little 7' is Bill; 26 is BRIDGE, so this is the Bailey bridge.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the surname in the song 'Bill Bailey' and of Donald Bailey, inventor of the Bailey bridge.

clue.text: See, Dr 7s is here! Can United invade the pitch?

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: invade means the abbreviation for United gets inside the word for pitch

parts.note: tar is pitch, the black sticky substance
U is a standard abbreviation for United, as in football club names

explanation.surface: A football fan wonders whether United's supporters can run on to the field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pitch' looks like a football field but is TAR. Cantuar is the Archbishop of Canterbury's signature; 7 is WILLIAM, and Dr Rowan Williams was archbishop when this puzzle ran.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin-derived signature names the See of Canterbury, where Dr Williams held office.

clue.text: Fundamental system derived from Old English argot

indicators.note: derived from means the letters are reworked to produce a new word

explanation.surface: A grammar is said to have grown out of an old English slang.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole set of a plant's roots is a fundamental system, quite literally at the base.

clue.text: Left one time, time and time again — one of the intelligentsia

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
an era is a period of time
an era is a period of time
an era is a period of time
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: An intellectual is described as leaving again and again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One of' does not define a single person here: its 'one' gives the final I, leaving 'the intelligentsia' as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Literary, learned people as a group are the intellectual class.

clue.text: Contract a bishop enters into immediately

indicators.note: enters into means the bishop's letters go inside the word for immediately

parts.note: now means immediately
RR stands for Right Reverend, a bishop's title

explanation.surface: A bishop signs an agreement straight away.
explanation.definitionFit: To narrow something is to make it contract or become smaller.

clue.text: Stewart including one French song

indicators.note: including means the French word sits inside the singer's first name

parts.note: Rod Stewart is the rock singer
un is French for one

explanation.surface: Rod Stewart sings a French number.
explanation.definitionFit: A canon in which voices enter in turn, like 'Frère Jacques', is a type of song.

clue.text: Get thee hence, Mr Thribb! Bend an ear in old Egypt and make, say, a vain attack!

parts.note: an archaic biblical way of saying depart
E.J. Thribb is Private Eye's spoof seventeen-year-old poet

indicators.note: in means the turned-round ear goes inside the old state's initials

parts.note: UAR, the United Arab Republic, was Egypt's name from 1958 to 1971

indicators.note: bend means the word for ear is bent back on itself

parts.note: lug is slang for an ear

explanation.surface: A rambling exclamation tells a poet to leave and listen in ancient Egypt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bend' turns LUG to GUL. Private Eye is a British satirical magazine. 'Vain' stands for 'vein', as 'say' warns: the jugular vein is in the neck.
explanation.definitionFit: To attack ferociously at the most vulnerable point means aiming at the neck's great vein.

clue.text: Almost certain to invade bad performance in this theatre of Becket, say?

indicators.note: to invade means the shortened word goes into the middle of the jumbled letters
performance suggests putting on a show with the letters, so they are rearranged
almost means the word for certain loses its last letter

parts.note: sure means certain

explanation.surface: A sure thing breaks into a poor stage show at a theatre staging Beckett.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' cuts SURE to SUR; 'performance' turns BAD into ABD. Samuel Beckett wrote for the Theatre of the Absurd; the spelling Becket teases with the archbishop St Thomas Becket.
explanation.definitionFit: Beckett's plays are classed as Theatre of the Absurd, the absurdist drama school.
